This strongly favors action 1 (up) and action 2 (down), mildly favors action 0 (no-op), leaves action 3 (left) near neutral, and strongly disfavors action 4 (right). The W1 rows are small and noisy, but they are not zero across the moving-object channel (channel 1) or previous-frame channel (channel 4), so the policy is using information about things that move and where they were on the previous step. The reward-target channel (channel 2) also has non-trivial weights, so reward location matters. The wall/obstacle channel (channel 3) is present but does not dominate the readable structure.

Reasoning: The action bias is the key clue. A policy that starts with a strong preference against moving right, while favoring up/down, fits a game where the agent begins moving rightward and must turn to avoid the right wall or its own body. A no-op bias that is slightly positive also fits a game where waiting can be safe or where no-op is not immediately fatal. Games like Sokoban, Pac-Man, or Zelda usually make no-op useless or harmful, so they are less likely. Boulderdash can use no-op to wait for falling objects, but it typically requires moving right as well, which conflicts with the strong negative bias on right. Snake fits best: the agent is a snake head, moving objects are the snake body, reward targets are food, obstacles are walls, and the previous-frame channel helps avoid self-collision and track body movement.

Game: Snake.

Description: The agent controls a snake head on a 10x10 grid, moving up/down/left/right to eat food. Eating food gives reward and grows the snake; the agent must avoid hitting the wall border or its own body.

Confidence: 70%
